title: Remediation SLA options + customer tier mapping (Hosted / Dedicated / Private) — working doc
content:
Doc purpose (Product Ops)
========================
We need a consistent set of internal remediation SLAs (time-to-mitigate / time-to-fix expectations) that:
- match what we can realistically execute across tiers (Hosted, Dedicated, Private)
- align with customer expectations and enterprise commitments (especially Dedicated/Private)
- can be implemented in tooling (ENG-4829 / SLA timers + breach alerts) without constant exceptions
- remains low-cardinality and understandable during live incidents

This is a working evaluation doc of options; final policy will live in Confluence in the Remediation SLA matrix.

Definitions
===========
- Remediation SLAs in this doc are internal operational targets and escalation triggers.
- We track two clocks:
  1) TTM (time-to-mitigate): time from incident declared (Sev assigned) to customer-impact mitigation in place (or credible workaround). Mitigation may include rollback, routing/fallback changes, traffic shaping, or isolating a bad region/model.
  2) TTF (time-to-fix): time from incident declared to a durable fix deployed OR a signed-off plan with committed ship date (depending on severity). For Sev0/Sev1, we typically expect a durable fix, not just a plan.

- “Tier” definitions:
  - Hosted: multi-tenant public API.
  - Dedicated: reserved capacity; stronger expectations for predictability and comms.
  - Private: VPC/on-prem control plane + data plane; sometimes customer-controlled networking and change windows.

- Severity (draft; matches on-call practice):
  - Sev0: broad outage / severe customer impact / safety risk / inability to serve core requests at scale.
  - Sev1: major degradation (e.g., high 5xx, severe latency) affecting meaningful customer set or a major enterprise customer; urgent.
  - Sev2: partial degradation; workarounds exist; limited scope.
  - Sev3: minor; limited impact; typically handled in normal on-call flow.

Decision principles
===================
1) Make the SLA actionable during incidents (what it forces us to do: staff, escalate, decide).
2) Keep differences by tier minimal, but acknowledge Dedicated/Private have different reality (capacity isolation, maintenance windows, customer networking).
3) Avoid a matrix so complex that incident-bot can’t enforce it.
4) “Pause/override” exists but must be auditable and rare.

Where tier differences are real (observations)
============================================
Hosted
- We control infra + routing + runtime deploys; can mitigate quickly via routing policies, throttles, or rollbacks.
- Customers accept “platform-wide” incidents but expect fast mitigation.

Dedicated
- Stronger expectations: named account pressure, high-touch comms, fewer acceptable repeated incidents.
- Mitigation sometimes means reallocating fleet capacity; can be constrained by GPU availability.
- Some mitigations require coordination with specific customer traffic patterns and agreed “degradation mode.”

Private
- Customer networking, DNS/TLS, firewalls, and change windows can dominate.
- “Mitigation” may require customer action; we can provide fix/instructions but can’t always execute.
- On-prem/air-gapped environments may block fast patching.

Key question: Do we set stricter SLAs for Dedicated/Private because customers pay more, or do we set realistic SLAs acknowledging dependencies and shift strictness into comms/escalation?

Option set
==========
Option A — Single SLA matrix (same targets across tiers) + comms escalation tiers
Pros: simple; consistent; easy to implement + dashboard.
Cons: risks being unrealistic for Private; breaches become noisy; forces frequent overrides.

Option B — Tier-adjusted TTF only (TTM consistent, TTF differs)
Pros: keeps the “stop the bleeding” behavior consistent; reflects reality that durable fixes take longer when customers control deploy windows.
Cons: still may be tight for certain Private classes; requires tier in SLA evaluator.

Option C — Tier-adjusted TTM and TTF (Dedicated stricter on TTM; Private looser on TTF)
Pros: matches customer expectation: Dedicated should be mitigated extremely fast; Private fixes can take longer.
Cons: more complex; risk of perceived unfairness (“why does private get longer?”).

Option D — Incident-type-aware SLA within severity (e.g., Private connectivity vs Control plane vs Runtime regression)
Pros: most accurate.
Cons: too complex for v1; high maintenance; taxonomy drift.

Recommendation (draft): Option B for v1
======================================
- Keep TTM targets consistent by severity across tiers (behavior we want in every incident: mitigate quickly).
- Allow tier-adjusted TTF targets (Private often needs customer maintenance window; Dedicated should still be fast but not necessarily faster than Hosted in all cases).
- In addition, define comms/escalation requirements by tier (Dedicated/Private proactive outreach thresholds), separate from remediation timers.

Proposed draft SLA targets (v1 candidate)
========================================
Notes:
- Times are proposed internal targets for breach alerting + leadership escalation.
- TTM measured to: restored SLO or reduced to acceptable degradation mode (documented).
- TTF measured to: fix deployed OR (Sev2/Sev3 only) fix scheduled with owner + date.

TTM (same across tiers)
-----------------------
Sev0: 30 minutes
Sev1: 2 hours
Sev2: 1 business day
Sev3: 5 business days (or next planned release train)

TTF (tier-adjusted)
-------------------
Hosted:
- Sev0: 24 hours
- Sev1: 3 business days
- Sev2: 10 business days
- Sev3: 30 business days

Dedicated:
- Sev0: 24 hours (same as Hosted; expectation is mitigation is faster, fix can be similar)
- Sev1: 5 business days (slightly longer than Hosted because some fixes involve fleet reshaping or customer-specific config review)
- Sev2: 15 business days
- Sev3: 30 business days

Private:
- Sev0: 48 hours (some fixes require customer coordination/change window; still want high urgency)
- Sev1: 10 business days
- Sev2: 20 business days
- Sev3: 45 business days

Rationale snapshots (to validate)
================================
- Private Sev0 TTF at 48h is the most controversial number. The intent is: if a Private incident is Sev0, we should be able to ship a fix quickly OR provide a validated workaround package quickly. But we may not be able to deploy it into the customer’s environment inside 48h. Proposed compromise: define “TTF = fix available” vs “TTF = deployed” for Private only.

Proposed adjustment for Private only:
- For Private tier: treat TTF as “fix available + customer delivery completed (artifact + instructions + support handoff)” rather than “fully deployed in customer environment.” Deployment tracking becomes a CS/Support deliverable.

This avoids constant SLA breaches from customer-controlled schedules, while still forcing Redwood to produce the fix quickly.

Edge cases + carve-outs (must be explicit)
=========================================
1) Cloud provider / upstream outage
- If root cause is confirmed upstream (AWS/GCP region/network, managed KMS outage, etc.):
  - TTM still applies (we should mitigate via failover/fallback where possible).
  - TTF may be waived or converted to “post-incident hardening actions” with due dates.
- Implementation requirement: incident-bot must allow “Upstream dependency” as a contributing factor and a “SLA exception reason” (audited).

2) Customer-caused or customer-controlled failures (mostly Private, occasionally Dedicated)
Examples:
- Customer rotated certs incorrectly; firewall blocks new endpoints; DNS misconfig; customer refuses recommended upgrade.
- TTM definition may be “workaround identified + communicated + support engaged.”
- TTF becomes a tracked action plan with customer owner and Redwood owner; SLA breach should not trigger paging.
- Implementation requirement: a controlled “Customer action required” exception reason.

3) Planned maintenance / change windows
- If incident is triggered by a planned change performed by Redwood:
  - SLAs still apply (we own it).
- If fix requires customer change window:
  - Private: allow “Fix available” measurement as above.

4) Multi-cause incidents
- Primary incident_type determines SLA class.
- Contributing systems recorded separately; do not create multiple SLA clocks.
- If reclassified, SLA clock should not reset (only severity changes reset behavior).

Comms and escalation requirements (separate from remediation timers)
===================================================================
We should not bake comms into remediation SLAs, but we do need consistent obligations by tier.

Draft comms rules (for CS alignment; see comms templates doc):
- Hosted
  - Sev0/Sev1: status page + initial update within 30 min; updates at least every 60 min until mitigated.
  - Sev2: case-by-case; internal update; status page optional.

- Dedicated
  - Sev0/Sev1: proactive outreach to affected accounts; initial customer-facing update within 30 min; updates every 60 min.
  - Sev2: proactive outreach within 1 business day if single account materially impacted.

- Private
  - Sev0/Sev1: proactive outreach; include “customer action required” assessment early.
  - Emphasize safe language: symptoms, mitigations, next update time.

Open issues / questions to resolve before signoff
=================================================
1) Private TTF definition: “available” vs “deployed”
- Need decision from SRE + Product Private (Vivek) + CS.

2) Dedicated Sev1 TTF: 3 vs 5 business days
- Dedicated product (Lauren) asked for realism: some changes require capacity rebalancing + canary.
- Counterpoint: enterprise expectation is faster. Maybe keep 3 BD but allow exceptions for capacity procurement work.

3) Severity-to-tier mapping clarity
- Can a Private incident be Sev0 if it affects only one customer? Yes, if it blocks core use case and is high urgency.
- Need crisp language in the incident process policy so on-call doesn’t under-severity enterprise incidents.

4) Implementation feasibility in tooling (ENG-4829)
- SLA evaluator needs tier + severity + type.
- Ensure we don’t create a combinatorial matrix. Proposed v1: severity x tier only, with optional overrides.

5) Reporting expectations
- Aisha to confirm dashboards will report:
  - SLA breach rate by tier, severity, incident_type
  - Exception counts by reason (upstream, customer-action, force majeure)

Data sanity check (informal)
============================
Based on last 2 quarters anecdotal review (see top-incidents analysis):
- Most Sev0/Sev1 mitigations happen within 15–90 minutes for Hosted when the mitigation is routing/rollback.
- Dedicated mitigations vary: quick when routing-only; slow when capacity constrained.
- Private “fix deployed” often exceeds 1–2 weeks due to customer windows; “fix available” is typically within a few days if we prioritize.

Action items (next steps)
=========================
- Rachel: circulate this doc to Rafael, Nikhil, Lauren, Vivek, Dev for comments (by 2026-02-07)
- Rafael/SRE: confirm if “TTF = plan w/ ship date” is acceptable for Sev2/Sev3 (Hosted/Dedicated) (by 2026-02-10)
- Vivek + CS: propose Private TTF measurement definition language for Confluence (by 2026-02-10)
- Lauren: confirm Dedicated Sev1 TTF target (3 vs 5 BD) and list top constraints (capacity procurement, release trains) (by 2026-02-12)
- Aisha: verify dashboards can label tier correctly and track exceptions without high cardinality (by 2026-02-12)

Appendix: quick matrix (for copy/paste)
======================================
TTM (all tiers):
- Sev0: 30m
- Sev1: 2h
- Sev2: 1 BD
- Sev3: 5 BD

TTF:
- Hosted:   Sev0 24h | Sev1 3 BD | Sev2 10 BD | Sev3 30 BD
- Dedicated:Sev0 24h | Sev1 5 BD | Sev2 15 BD | Sev3 30 BD
- Private:  Sev0 48h | Sev1 10 BD| Sev2 20 BD | Sev3 45 BD

Appendix: proposed SLA exception reasons (allowlist)
===================================================
- Upstream dependency confirmed (cloud/provider)
- Customer action required (customer-controlled environment)
- Force majeure (rare; requires Director+ approval)
- Mis-severity (initial severity incorrect; adjust and document)

(End)
